body.statement: For each fixed \(t\) and cell \(x\), the sharp extrema of \(\nu_x(D(0)>t,R(1)\le r)\) are \(A^L_x(r,t)\) and \(A^U_x(r,t)\). One coupling attains \(A^U_x(r,t)\) simultaneously for every \(r\le t\), and another coupling attains \(A^L_x(r,t)\) simultaneously for every \(r\le t\). Therefore the standardized coordinate bounds follow by summing with weights \(p_x/S(t)\), and the sharp RM-SACE interval is obtained by integrating the opposite common TV-SACE envelopes along that fixed cohort.
body.justification: Coordinatewise sharpness does not justify integration; common extremizers are the missing mathematical reason that fixed-cohort RM-SACE envelope integration is exact.
body.gap: Chen, Cui, and Yang integrate threshold bounds for a scalar survivor outcome, while the opened papers do not prove one coupling jointly attains all readmission thresholds for a nested survivor cohort.
body.consumer: It gives a closed-form RM-SACE sensitivity region without solving a new optimization problem at every integration point.
body.proof_tex:
The proof uses nested-deadline matching, suffix cuts, and compact limiting.  Fix \(x\) and \(t\), write \(s=s_x(t)\), and extend the treated survivor kernel by the boundary convention \(K_x(\infty,B)=0\).  If \(s=0\), the cut at \(\infty\) makes both deadline ranks zero, and the assertion is immediate.  Assume henceforth that \(s>0\).

For any compatible full law, let \(w\) be the treated-record submeasure selected by \(D(0)>t\):
\[
 w(H)=\Pr\{(D(1),R(1))\in H,D(0)>t\mid X=x\}.
\]
It has mass \(s\), is dominated by \(\mu_{1x}\), is supported on \(D(1)>t\), and terminal monotonicity gives, for every \(u\geq t\),
\[
 w(D(1)>u)\geq\Pr(D(0)>u\mid X=x)=s_x(u).                             \tag{12}
\]
For a Borel mark set \(B\), split selected records at deadline \(u\).  At most \(s-s_x(u)\) selected records can lie at or before \(u\), by (12), and at most \(K_x(u,B)\) available \(B\)-records lie after \(u\).  Hence
\[
 w(R(1)\in B)\leq s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B),
\]
including the boundary cut \(u=\infty\).  Taking the infimum proves the upper deadline bound.

We next prove sharpness on a finite rational grid.  Multiply all masses by a common denominator.  Make one demand copy for each unit of control mass with \(D(0)>t\), and one resource copy for each unit of treated mass with \(D(1)>t\).  Join a demand of death level \(i\) to a resource of level \(h\) exactly when \(i\leq h\).  Taking the full mark set in the capacity inequalities gives every suffix inequality
\[
 \#\{\text{resources of level greater than }u\}
 \geq \#\{\text{demands of level greater than }u\}.                \tag{13}
\]
Sorting demands from latest to earliest and assigning at each step an unused admissible resource proves by induction from (13) that all demands can be matched.

For resources whose marks lie in \(B\), run the usual alternating-path augmentation, which is elementary here because neighborhoods are nested suffixes.  If augmentation stops, the demands reachable by alternating paths may be replaced by the suffix beginning at their earliest death level without enlarging their resource neighborhood.  Absence of an augmenting path then partitions every matched \(B\)-resource into either a resource used by a demand outside that suffix or a \(B\)-resource adjacent to the suffix.  At the stopping suffix \(u\), equality holds in
\[
 \#\{\text{matched \(B\)-resources}\}
 \leq \#\{\text{demands at or before }u\}
      +\#\{\text{available \(B\)-resources after }u\}.             \tag{14}
\]
The right side is the scaled value \(s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B)\).  Conversely, (14) is valid for every matching and every suffix, as already proved.  Thus the maximum number of selected \(B\)-resources equals the minimum deadline cut.  Superposing a maximizing partial matching with a full matching and augmenting along their alternating paths and cycles extends it to a full matching without deleting a selected \(B\)-resource.

The matchable subsets of resources satisfy augmentation: if one matchable set is smaller than another, superpose their matchings; an alternating path starting from a resource used only by the larger matching augments the smaller one.  Order resources by increasing readmission category and greedily accept a resource whenever the accepted set remains matchable.  After every prefix, augmentation implies that the accepted set has maximum possible size within that prefix.  Extending the final accepted set to a matching of all survivor demands gives one selected submeasure that attains the deadline-cut maximum simultaneously for every readmission prefix.  Reversing the mark order maximizes every complementary suffix and therefore simultaneously minimizes every prefix.

It remains to pair the unselected treated records with the control deaths at or before \(t\).  Write \(T_x(u)=\Pr(D(1)>u\mid X=x)\).  For \(u\leq t\), every selected resource has \(D(1)>t\), so its tail mass at \(u\) is \(s\); the residual treated tail is \(T_x(u)-s\), whereas the residual control tail is \(s_x(u)-s\).  Marginal terminal dominance, obtained by taking the full mark set in the survivor-capacity inequality, gives
\[
 T_x(u)-s\geq s_x(u)-s.
\]
For \(u>t\), the residual control tail is zero.  Sorting both residual collections from latest to earliest and applying the same suffix induction therefore completes the matching without changing the selected cohort.  Thus every extremizing selected matching extends to a full terminal-monotone coupling.

For arbitrary real finite masses, approximate the complete finite table by rational tables on the same allowed cells.  The rational extremizers lie in a fixed finite simplex.  A convergent subsequence preserves nonnegativity, both margins, and the closed order constraint, while every finite cut and objective converges.  This proves the same formula and common-prefix conclusion for real finite tables.

For continuous time, take nested finite partitions containing \(t\) and any prescribed finite collection of readmission thresholds, isolate \(\infty\), and retain the within-cell order relation.  Apply the finite result to the coarsened margins and take full-law lifts furnished by the quadratic chain theorem.  The compact-carrier lemma gives a weakly convergent subsequence.  Its limit has the original within-arm margins and the closed order \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The density envelope implies zero mass at every finite threshold and, for \(u<v\),
\[
 |K_x(u,B)-K_x(v,B)|
 \leq\Pr\{u<D(1)\leq v\mid X=x\}\leq M|u-v|.                       \tag{15}
\]
The analogous bound holds for \(s_x\).  Consequently the discrete suffix minima converge to the continuum infimum, and the limiting coupling attains the extrema at every threshold in the prescribed finite collection.

Inside the compact fixed-margin full-law fiber, the set of couplings attaining the upper value at a given finite \(r\) is closed: the objective boundary is contained in \(\{D(0)=t\}\cup\{R(1)=r\}\), which has probability zero by the fixed finite-part marginal densities.  The preceding finite-threshold construction gives these closed optimizing sets the finite-intersection property.  Compactness therefore supplies one coupling attaining the upper value for every \(r\leq t\).  Reversing the readmission order supplies one lower coupling for all such \(r\).

Taking \(B=[0,r]\) identifies the upper endpoint as \(A_x^U(r,t)\).  Applying the upper formula to \(B=(r,\infty]\) and subtracting from the total selected mass gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \min_\nu\nu_x(D(0)>t,R(1)\leq r)
 &=s-\inf_u\{s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}\\
 &=\sup_u\{s_x(u)-K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}=A_x^L(r,t).                   \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
For a fixed cohort \(t\), choose the common extremizer separately in each of the finitely many covariate cells.  Since \(p_x/S(t)\geq0\) and \(S(t)\geq\eta>0\) on the target domain, summing the cell endpoints and subtracting the fixed \(b_x(r,t)\) gives the sharp standardized TV-SACE envelopes \(\theta^L\) and \(\theta^U\).

Finally, every compatible surface obeys \(\theta^L(r,t)\leq\theta_\nu(r,t)\leq\theta^U(r,t)\).  The RM-surface definition gives
\[
 -\int_0^a\theta^U(r,t)\,dr
 \leq\rho_\nu(a,t)\leq
 -\int_0^a\theta^L(r,t)\,dr.                                       \tag{17}
\]
The common upper and lower couplings attain the left and right endpoints of (17), respectively.  Thus fixed-cohort RM integration is sharp because of common extremizers, not merely because every TV coordinate is separately sharp.
